newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Osem still eyeing Middle East investments.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Osem still eyeing Middle East investments.

text.p: Osem Investments, Israel's second largest publicly traded food company, is still seeking joint ventures in the Middle East, Gad Propper, managing director of Osem's international subsidiary, said on Monday.
"We are definitely looking for things," he told Reuters at a conference on Middle development at Bar Ilan University outside of Tel Aviv.
Osem recently abandoned plans to acquire a 50 percent stake in an unidentified Egyptian company for $7.5 million. Propper said the decision to end talks was not connected with politics.
Propper said Nestle, which acquired 40 percent of Osem earlier this year, had not decided whether it could use the Israeli company as its "hub" for the Middle East.
"They came here primarily for the Israeli market," he said. "But they are heavily active in neighbouring countries."
Propper said it was tougher for Israeli companies like Osem that sell consumer goods to enter Arab markets because ordinary people were still resistant to trade with Israel.

"From the people themselves, the ups and downs we have in the peace process are not always seen, as I put it, as a natural process," he said. "I wouldn't dare to say what would or could happen to an Israeli product if it were there when there was a big down."

Propper said his 75 percent-owned Interbeauty Ltd faced the same problems in trying to sell the L'Oreal cosmetics products it manufactures to Middle East markets. "We are discussing now about selling to Turkey...and one of the first questions that came up there was does 'Made in Israel' mean something bad (to consumers) in Turkey or not," he said.

Muzi Wertheim, chairman of United Mizrahi Bank and Central Bottling Co, the Israeli Coca Cola bottler, said he rejected a plan to build a joint venture ceramics factory in the Palestinian-controlled Gaza Strip. Instead, the plant was built in Jordan.
"The reason we didn't do business in Gaza was because there was no administration to turn to," he explained. But, he said, he believed the situation had improved.
"I have reason to believe after talking to Palestinians this week that proper business plans (in the future) will be approved within 24 hours," Wertheimer explained.

The Jordanian plant, a joint venture with a Jordanian-Palestinian family he refused to name, is located near Amman. The plant uses Italian know-how and raw materials to make mosaics, artistic tiles and stone profiles.
"We have not forsaken our wish to invest in Gaza and I am sure we will," Wertheinm said.
